findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: int order() is added to the public CryptoProvider interface as an abstract method with no default. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now invokes CryptoProvider::order on every provider discovered via ServiceLoader, so any third-party CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous interface will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime as soon as provider detection runs, and will fail to compile when rebuilt. keycloak-common is consumed by client applications and custom crypto integrations (e.g. custom FIPS providers) implement this interface, so this is a binary- and source-incompatible change. Make it a default method, e.g. default int order() { return 0; }, so existing implementations keep working.

findings.title: Ties between providers with equal top order are now silently resolved by classpath order
findings.body: detectProvider now sorts providers by order() descending and returns the first one; for providers with equal order the stable sort keeps ServiceLoader (i.e. JAR/classpath) order. Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath was a hard IllegalStateException with a clear message. All three server providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return order 200, so a misconfigured classpath containing e.g. both keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402 no longer fails fast: one is picked based on opaque JAR ordering and the deployment can silently run with the wrong (possibly non-FIPS) crypto provider, with only a DEBUG-level message listing the ignored providers. Consider failing, or at least logging at WARN level, when more than one provider shares the highest order.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK default keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The interface contract states this method returns the BouncyCastle security provider (FIPS or non-FIPS). This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the provider backing the JVM's default keystore type (typically the SUN provider) and has nothing to do with BouncyCastle. Any caller that relies on the contract — for example code that registers the returned provider or requests BC algorithms from it via BouncyIntegration — will fail with confusing NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider errors or silently use the wrong provider. Since nearly every other method of this class throws UnsupportedOperationException, and WildFlyElytronProvider returns null for this same method, this method should do one of those instead of returning a misleading provider.

findings.title: Dead code: two discarded ASN1Encoder writes in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 call ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger) and immediately discard the results; the actual DER sequence returned is built from two separate, freshly created encoders in the return statement. These two calls are leftover dead code that serve no purpose and can confuse readers of signature-conversion code; they should be removed.
